strengths: Addresses a practical problem: reducing the cost of continual classification with frozen pretrained backbones. The pipeline is straightforward and avoids exemplar storage and backbone updates.

Reports a promising accuracy–efficiency tradeoff across five datasets, two backbone architectures, longer task sequences, and an online setting. For example, on CUB with ViT-B/16, Fly-CL achieves 93.84% average accuracy versus RanPAC’s 92.67%, with substantially lower reported training time.
Includes five-seed results, component timing measurements, memory comparisons, ablations, and sensitivity analyses. These provide useful empirical evidence beyond a single benchmark.
weaknesses: The top-k guarantee is not established. Assumption B.2 essentially assumes the desired energy retention without demonstrating it for the proposed random features. Moreover, a bound on the expected retained-energy fraction does not imply the unnormalized expectation bound in Theorem B.4. The claimed decay with expansion dimension also neglects that the unscaled projection has E||Wv||² = mp||v||²/d under uniform random supports, which grows with m. Consequently, k = Ω(m^α) alone does not establish vanishing loss degradation.

Theorem 4.1’s proof applies a random-matrix determinant result after checking only entry means and variances. Exactly p nonzeros per row introduces dependence between entries, and the proof does not verify the cited theorem’s hypotheses or specify sufficient scaling conditions on p. Sparse square submatrices can have zero columns. The stated high-probability invertibility guarantee therefore lacks a valid justification.

The central efficiency comparison does not sufficiently isolate algorithmic advances from standard numerical improvements. Sparse random features, ridge sufficient statistics, GCV, and Cholesky solves are established techniques. An optimized RanPAC baseline using reusable spectral decompositions or appropriate dual solves, matched regularization search, and Cholesky factorization is needed. Comparing against repeated O(lm³) inversions leaves uncertainty about how much speedup is specific to Fly-CL.

GCV in Equations 8–11 evaluates a ridge model trained only on the current task, whereas the deployed classifier uses accumulated statistics from all tasks. Thus, it selects regularization for a different estimator and distribution. The paper neither justifies this mismatch nor compares current-task GCV with cumulative validation, fixed regularization, or other selection strategies in accuracy and forgetting.

The progressive-decorrelation explanation is stronger than the evidence. Linear expansion alone cannot improve linear separability, and ridge regression does not generally guarantee decorrelated classifier columns. Figure 3 shows correlations for only ten selected prototypes; the theoretical results concern information retention rather than progressive decorrelation. Controlled comparisons of top-k versus ReLU, dense versus sparse projection, and their interaction with ridge regression would better establish the proposed mechanism.

The resource and evaluation claims need stronger controls. The method still stores an O(m²) Gram matrix and performs O(m³) factorization; Table 4 omits a separate timing for Gram accumulation. Low-latency deployment claims are not supported by end-to-end per-sample inference measurements. F-OAL’s collapse to 26.15% on ResNet-50/VTAB warrants numerical-stability and tuning checks rather than an untested attribution to accumulated errors.

Reproducibility is incomplete: the code URL is missing, checkpoint and dataset links are placeholders, and the regularization-grid size and online batch protocol are unspecified. Table 11 uses a nonstandard CUB train/test split without explaining its construction, making comparison with established results difficult.

Provides five-seed results, component timing measurements, memory comparisons, ablations, and hyperparameter sensitivity analyses.
weaknesses: The sparsification theory has substantive gaps. Appendix B.4 incorrectly derives an expected absolute residual-energy bound from an expected relative-energy bound without controlling dependence on the total norm. The claimed dimension-dependent decay also requires bounded embedding energy; under the stated unscaled projection, E||Wv||² = mp||v||²/d, which grows with m for fixed input and connectivity.

Theorem 4.1 is insufficiently justified. Matching entry means and variances does not establish applicability of the cited determinant theorem to matrices with exactly p nonzeros per row and dependent support indicators. No required scaling of p with d is specified; sparse square submatrices can contain zero columns.

The contribution is largely a combination of established sparse random features, top-k selection, accumulated ridge statistics, GCV, and Cholesky factorization. Crucially, there is no matched RanPAC baseline equipped with the same GCV and Cholesky optimizations, leaving unclear how much advantage comes from the proposed representation versus reusable implementation improvements.

The decorrelation explanation exceeds the evidence. Linear expansion alone cannot improve linear separability, and low correlations among classifier columns do not establish improved classification or resolved feature multicollinearity. Figure 3 shows only ten selected prototypes; the theorems concern information preservation rather than progressive decorrelation.

GCV is computed using only the current task’s features and labels, whereas the selected regularization is applied to cumulative statistics from all tasks. This mismatch is neither theoretically justified nor evaluated against cumulative-data selection or a tuned fixed regularizer, particularly under heterogeneous task distributions.

Efficiency claims need clearer qualification. The method still stores an O(m²) Gram matrix and performs O(m³) factorization at every update. Table 4 omits Gram accumulation and top-k selection as separate costs, and experiments on an RTX 3090 do not establish suitability for resource-constrained edge deployment.

Reproducibility is incomplete: the code URL is absent, checkpoint and dataset entries are only unlinked 'Link' placeholders, and the nonstandard CUB split of 9,430 training and 2,358 evaluation images is not explained. These details matter for interpreting the unusually strong results and reproducing the comparisons.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically important problem: reducing the computational cost of continual learning with frozen pretrained representations. The proposed pipeline is straightforward and compatible with both transformer and CNN backbones.

Reported accuracy–runtime trade-offs are promising. On ViT-B/16, Fly-CL achieves 93.84% on CUB and 96.54% on VTAB, with substantially lower training times than the evaluated baselines; CIFAR-100 accuracy remains close to RanPAC.

The evaluation includes five datasets, two backbones, longer task sequences, an online setting, and five-seed results. Memory measurements, component timings, and hyperparameter sensitivity analyses provide useful additional evidence.
Accumulating sufficient statistics supports exemplar-free learning, and using GCV and Cholesky factorization is a sensible practical approach to accelerating ridge classification.
weaknesses: The top-k theoretical guarantee is not established. Assumption B.2 bounds an expected retained-energy fraction, but Theorem B.4 incorrectly converts this into a bound on expected absolute residual energy without additional assumptions. Moreover, the claimed vanishing error for k = Ω(m^α) requires controlling E[||h||²], which generally grows with m under the specified unnormalized random projection. The assumed strong energy concentration is neither derived for these features nor empirically verified.

Theorem 4.1 also lacks a valid justification. Matching entry means and variances does not establish applicability of the cited random-matrix determinant theorem: fixing exactly p nonzeros per row introduces dependence. The statement lacks explicit support-sampling and sparsity-growth conditions needed to exclude singular submatrices, including those with empty columns. These are substantive gaps in the advertised theoretical support.

The efficiency comparisons do not sufficiently isolate the proposed representation from standard numerical optimizations. GCV, spectral reuse, and Cholesky solves could also accelerate competing ridge-based methods. Table 4 compares against repeated inversion and LU-based implementations, but an optimized RanPAC baseline with matched backbone adaptation, regularization search, and solvers is needed to establish the distinctive contribution.

The GCV criterion evaluates a classifier fitted only on the current task, whereas the selected regularization parameter is applied to the cumulative classifier. This is a heuristic for the actual continual-learning objective, with no direct validation of its effect on previously learned classes. An accuracy comparison against fixed regularization and validation-based selection is missing.

The mechanistic claims exceed the evidence. Linear random expansion alone cannot improve linear separability; any such improvement requires the nonlinear stage. Ridge regression also does not generally guarantee decorrelated class weights. The selected ten-class correlation visualization supports an observation, but does not establish the claimed general progressive-decorrelation mechanism or its causal relationship to accuracy.

Important evaluation and reproducibility details remain unresolved. The reported CUB split of 9,430/2,358 differs from the standard split and needs justification and an exact protocol. The severe ResNet-50 collapse of F-OAL is attributed to numerical error without diagnostic evidence. Online batch size and regularization-selection details are insufficiently specified. Finally, the method still stores an m-by-m Gram matrix and performs cubic Cholesky factorization, limiting the broader claims about lightweight deployment and scalability.

strengths: The paper addresses a useful practical problem: reducing the cost of continual classification with frozen pretrained backbones. The implementation combines sparse random features, top-k activation, adaptive ridge regularization, and efficient linear solves in a coherent pipeline.

Reported accuracy–runtime trade-offs are promising. On ViT-B/16, Fly-CL achieves 93.84% average accuracy on CUB versus RanPAC's 92.67%, while reducing post-extraction training time from 33.83 to 0.35 seconds per task. CIFAR-100 accuracy remains close to RanPAC with substantially lower runtime.

The empirical coverage is reasonably broad: five datasets, CNN and transformer backbones, longer task sequences, online experiments, and an additional foundation-model backbone. Five-seed results, memory measurements, component timings, and hyperparameter sensitivity analyses are valuable.
weaknesses: The sparse-matrix guarantee in Theorem 4.1 is not established. Appendix B.1 invokes a random-matrix determinant result after matching only entry means and variances, without verifying its distributional and independence assumptions; exactly p nonzeros per row creates dependent entries. The theorem also omits a necessary scaling regime for p relative to d. For fixed p and increasing d, a d-by-d submatrix has uncovered columns with high probability, contradicting the stated general guarantee.

The top-k guarantee has substantive mathematical gaps. Assumption B.2 bounds an expected retained-energy fraction, but this does not imply the expected absolute residual-energy bound used in Theorem B.4 without additional assumptions. Furthermore, the claimed decay for k = Ω(m^α) ignores the growth of E[||h||²]: under the specified unnormalized projection, E_W[||Wv||²] = mp||v||²/d. The required energy-concentration assumption is also neither proved nor empirically verified for these random features.

The central progressive-decorrelation interpretation exceeds the evidence. Preserving rank or pairwise distances does not establish reduced class correlation, and ridge regularization does not generally produce decorrelated classifier columns. Figure 3 provides an illustrative heatmap rather than a general guarantee or a quantitative demonstration that decorrelation causes the accuracy improvements.

The efficiency comparison needs stronger controls. GCV and Cholesky factorization are standard techniques that could also accelerate RanPAC. Comparing against repeated matrix inversions does not isolate the benefit of the proposed representation. An optimized RanPAC baseline with the same numerical solver and regularization-selection machinery, plus matched sparse/dense and top-k/ReLU ablations, is needed to establish the contribution beyond implementation improvements.

GCV selects regularization using only the current task's features and labels, whereas the resulting classifier uses accumulated statistics from all tasks. Thus, the selection criterion evaluates a different estimator from the deployed classifier. The paper does not justify this approximation or measure its effect on earlier classes, especially under heterogeneous tasks and online batches.

The biological equivalence in Section 6 is overstated. The update is the familiar gradient rule for regularized squared loss, and deriving its stationary point does not establish convergence to the accumulated-data solution under a changing, replay-free stream. The section also switches from summed statistics to expectations without adjusting regularization, so the claimed exact correspondence requires a normalization correction.

Novelty and reproducibility remain insufficiently resolved. Closely related fly-inspired continual learning is cited but not directly compared, while the main ingredients are established methods. Appendix E leaves important details unclear, including the nonstandard CUB train/test split, online batch protocol, regularization-grid resolution, and sparse-kernel and timing implementation. These details matter particularly because runtime is the main claimed advantage.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant practical problem: reducing the cost of continual classification with pretrained representations. The pipeline is straightforward and maintains cumulative sufficient statistics without storing exemplars.

The reported accuracy–runtime trade-offs are promising. On ViT-B/16, Fly-CL achieves 93.84% on CUB and 96.54% on VTAB, with substantially lower training times than the evaluated baselines, while remaining competitive on CIFAR-100.

The empirical evaluation is reasonably broad: five datasets, transformer and CNN backbones, online learning, longer task sequences, memory measurements, component ablations, and five-seed results. The appendix also explores a larger vision encoder.
weaknesses: The top-k guarantee is not established. Assumption B.2 bounds the expected fraction of discarded energy, but this does not imply the expected absolute-energy bound in Theorem B.4 without additional assumptions about its dependence on total energy. Moreover, the claimed decay with increasing m ignores the growth of E[||h||²]: for the specified unnormalized projection, E_W[||Wv||²] = mp||v||²/d. Thus k = Ω(m^α) alone does not yield the stated vanishing bound. The strong energy-concentration assumption is also not verified for the actual projected features.

The full-rank argument in Theorem 4.1/Appendix B.1 is incomplete. Matching entry means and variances is insufficient to invoke a random-matrix determinant theorem; selecting exactly p nonzeros per row creates dependencies, and the necessary sparsity scaling is unspecified. Even with p growing slowly, square submatrices can contain zero columns with substantial probability. The paper needs a theorem whose assumptions match its construction.

The central efficiency comparison does not isolate the proposed representation from standard numerical improvements. GCV, decomposition reuse across regularization candidates, and Cholesky solves can also accelerate existing ridge-based methods. Table 4 compares against repeated inversions and LU, but there is no matched RanPAC baseline using the same optimized solver, feature adaptation policy, and regularization search. Consequently, the reported speedups do not establish how much benefit comes specifically from Fly-CL. The complete algorithm also retains cubic factorization and quadratic Gram-matrix storage.

The novelty is limited and insufficiently positioned. Sparse random expansion and winner-take-all coding are established fly-inspired techniques, while cumulative ridge statistics, GCV, and Cholesky factorization are standard tools. The paper needs a clearer distinction from the cited fly-inspired continual-learning work by Zou et al. (2025b), alongside controlled comparisons showing that the combination contributes more than implementation optimization.

The adaptive regularization criterion does not evaluate the classifier actually deployed. Equations 8–11 compute GCV using only the current task, whereas Equation 6 fits cumulative statistics from all tasks. This may be a useful heuristic, but its suitability for retaining previous classes is neither justified nor isolated experimentally. Comparisons against fixed regularization and a cumulative-data criterion are needed.

The biological and decorrelation claims exceed the analysis. Section 6 recovers ridge regression by writing gradient descent on a regularized squared-error objective as Hebbian and anti-Hebbian terms. This does not establish decorrelation or equivalence to sequential local learning without replay: stationary expectations and cumulative historical statistics are different settings, and the switch from sums to expectations also changes regularization scaling. Likewise, linear expansion alone cannot improve linear separability; that benefit requires the nonlinear stage.

Important evaluation details remain unresolved. Table 13 gives a nonstandard CUB training/evaluation split of 9,430/2,358 without explaining its construction, and the 50-class VTAB subset is insufficiently specified. The severe F-OAL degradation on ResNet-50 is attributed to numerical error without diagnostic evidence. These issues limit confidence in comparability and reproducibility despite the otherwise extensive experiments.

strengths: The paper addresses a practically relevant problem: reducing the cost of continual classification with frozen pretrained encoders. Sparse random features, top-k activation, and an analytic classifier form a straightforward, backbone-compatible pipeline.

The reported accuracy–runtime trade-offs are promising. On ViT-B/16, Fly-CL achieves 93.84% on CUB and 96.54% on VTAB, while reducing post-extraction training time substantially relative to RanPAC and F-OAL.

The empirical evaluation covers five datasets, transformer and CNN backbones, longer task sequences, and an online setting, with results averaged over five seeds. Memory measurements, component timing, ablations, and sensitivity studies provide useful additional evidence.
weaknesses: The central theoretical guarantees have substantive gaps. Theorem 4.1 applies a random-matrix determinant result based only on matching means and variances, without establishing its applicability to dependent entries induced by exactly p nonzeros per row. It also lacks a growth condition relating p to d; sparse square submatrices can have empty columns and be singular. Consequently, the claimed high-probability guarantee is not established.

The top-k guarantee in Theorem 4.2 is unsupported for the actual features. Appendix B assumes that almost all energy lies in the largest k coordinates without demonstrating this for Gaussian random projections. Furthermore, a bound on the expected retained-energy fraction does not imply the stated bound on expected discarded energy without additional assumptions. The claimed decay with m also ignores that E[||Wv||²] = mp||v||²/d for the specified unnormalized projection, which grows with m.

Novelty and the source of the speed gains are insufficiently isolated. Random expansion followed by ridge classification is already central to the closest baselines, while GCV and Cholesky factorization are established techniques. A decisive comparison would apply these solver optimizations to RanPAC under matched features, regularization ranges, and adaptation settings, then separately measure the contribution of sparse projection and top-k. Table 4 compares against a vanilla implementation but does not resolve this attribution issue. The closely related fly-inspired continual-learning work by Zou et al. (2025b) also needs a substantive comparison.

The adaptive regularization criterion does not evaluate the classifier actually deployed. Equations 8–11 select lambda using a ridge fit on only the current task, whereas Equation 6 fits accumulated statistics from all tasks. The paper provides neither a justification nor an ablation showing that this task-local criterion selects suitable regularization for past and current classes, especially in the online setting.

The progressive-decorrelation interpretation is stronger than the evidence. A linear expansion alone cannot improve linear separability; any improvement requires the subsequent nonlinearity. Ridge regression stabilizes estimation but does not generally guarantee decorrelated prototypes. Section 6 derives the familiar stationary point of regularized squared-error learning, rather than proving decorrelation or equivalence under a changing continual-learning distribution; it also switches from summed statistics to expectations without adjusting regularization.

Reproducibility and efficiency reporting need clarification. Table 13 uses a nonstandard CUB split of 9,430 training and 2,358 validation images without explaining its construction. Timing methodology lacks synchronization and hardware-allocation details, and Table 4 omits the accumulated Gram-matrix update explicitly costed in Algorithm 1. The method still stores an O(m²) matrix and performs an O(m³) factorization at each update, limiting the broader low-latency and resource-constrained deployment claims.
